newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa snaps higher at close after early slip.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa snaps higher at close after early slip.

text.p: London cocoa prices flipped up on Monday afternoon, ending higher across the board and within striking distance of last week's peak of 1,033 stg basis May.
"It's another backwards and forwards day," commented one trader.

The market turned around from an intraday low of 1,004 stg after trade buyers returned in late session. Sterling's weakness and arbitrage deals against New York may have also helped to push prices up. Phibro was said to be a good buyer.
May cocoa ended the day nine stg higher at 1,029 stg a tonne while further forwards racked up steeper gains with July up 13 stg at 1,040.
But turnover was a modest 5,982 lots, mostly on May.
Ghana purchases came in line with the latest pattern of figures with the cumulative reaching 291,788 tonnes by February 20. Arrivals were 5,072 tonnes in the 19th week.
The market's gyrations on Monday support the view that prices are consolidating recent gains although the overall trend remains upward.
But some traders argued the rally was only temporary.
"The cocoa market typically undergoes a period of price volatility at this time of year, but then tends to settle down and resumes its sideways pattern," said Merrill Lynch in a monthly report.
It saw little reason for the New York May contract to hold levels over $1,400 as origin selling was likely to intensify and manufacturers were not apt to extend coverage.
But a major uncertainty for the market is the size of the Ivorian crop.
Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze said last week the total crop would be less than one million tonnes but trade projections are significantly higher.
One leading UK-based analyst said on Monday the harvest was likely to total 1.070 million tonnes, including about 970,000 tonnes main crop.
The midcrop could be below average at around 100,000 however due to exceptionally dry weather in February.
"The midcrop is likely to be significantly below average, but not less than 100,000 tonnes," said the forecaster, who did not wish to be named.
Quiet conditions continued in the physical market although prices have recovered alongside the futures.
"Last week the industry got a bit worried. They were doing some price fixation and short covering. But then the market started to ease and they sat back again," said one trader.
